title: Private Deployments: VPC & On‑Prem Deployment Checklist and Day‑2 Ops Guide
author: Sofia Martinez
body:
Overview:

This page consolidates VPC and on‑prem deployment checklists, reference architectures, packaging guidance, and day‑2 operational procedures (monitoring, backups, scaling) for Redwood Private deployments. It is intended for platform engineers, SREs, and solutions engineers running Redwood in a customer VPC or on their premises.

Audience:
- Platform / SRE engineers
- Solutions / deployment engineers supporting private customers
- Customer IT/security teams with deployment responsibilities

Scope:
- VPC deployments (Cloud-hosted control plane with customer VPC peering/VPN/PrivateLink)
- On‑prem deployments (air‑gapped or within customer datacenter using the on‑prem package)
- Day‑2 operations: upgrades, rollback, patching, backups, monitoring, incident playbooks

Prerequisites (must be validated before kick-off):
| Item | Minimum requirement | Owner | Verification |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Network connectivity | BGP/VPN or PrivateLink with required ports (see network section) | Customer / Network | Ping, traceroute, TLS handshake 
| DNS | Internal DNS entries for control-plane and nodes | Customer | nslookup / dig 
| Certificates | CA and SANs for internal services (or integrate ACM/KMS) | Security / Customer | openssl s_client -connect ... 
| Storage | Block volumes with recommended IOPS (see infra table) | Infra | fio benchmark 
| Machine types | CPU/GPU, memory consistent with model profiles | Solutions | Instance inventory / gpu-smi 

Network and Firewall requirements (minimum):
- Control plane <-> customer VPC: TCP 443, 8443 (control APIs), 5000-5100 (optional agent ports).
- Worker nodes: allow outbound TLS to control-plane endpoints and image registries.
- Health checks: enable HTTP/HTTPS to /health endpoints from monitoring CIDRs.
- Peering considerations: ensure routes for KV cache endpoints and object storage.

Reference architectures (short):
1) VPC (recommended for most customers):
- Control plane hosted by Redwood in region X (multi-AZ)
- Customer VPC with private subnets for worker nodes
- Transit gateway/PrivateLink for secure connectivity
- NAT Gateways for OS/agent patching and container image pulls
- Managed object store (S3/GCS) for model artifacts and backups

2) On‑Prem (air‑gapped option):
- Customer provides hardware or VM cluster (K8s or bare metal)
- On‑prem package: OCI images + tarball bundle + offline package registry
- Local object store (MinIO) or NFS for model artifacts
- Optional egress-proxy for controlled updates

Hardware and capacity planning (table):
| Component | Recommendation (starting point) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Inference worker (single model) | 8 x A10G / T4 equivalent | ~16-30 RPS for short sequences (depends on model) |
| CPU-only workers | 24 vCPU, 128GB RAM | For embedding-only workloads |
| KV cache | 1 x 64 GB RAM per 8 workers | Adjust for context size |
| Storage | 1 TB NVMe per worker | Holds model shards and swap/cache |

On‑prem packaging and installation:
- Distribution: Docker/OCI images hosted on a registry (public or customer-hosted) plus release manifest (SHA256) and installation bundle (tar.gz).
- Installer: `redwood-install` (bash wrapper) or Helm chart for K8s-based installs.
- Authentication: integrate with customer KMS/HSM for master key, or use Redwood-managed keys for hybrid setups.
- Steps (high-level):
  1. Validate node prerequisites (OS, kernel, drivers).
  2. Install container runtime (containerd 1.8+ recommended) and GPU drivers (NVIDIA driver 525+ + nvidia-container-toolkit).
  3. Load offline images into local registry (if air‑gapped): `ctr images import` or `docker load`.
  4. Apply Helm chart or systemd units to start control-plane agents and worker services.

Example systemd unit (on-host agent):
[Unit]
Description=Redwood Onprem Agent
After=network.target

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/redwood-agent --config /etc/redwood/agent.yaml
Restart=on-failure
LimitNOFILE=65536

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

Day‑2 operations (runbooks):
- Health checks and regular maintenance:
  - Daily: verify node health, disk usage, GPU temperature; check agent heartbeats.
  - Weekly: OS and driver security patches in a canary pool.
  - Monthly: full cluster resource audit and model artifact backup.
- Monitoring and alerts (recommended metrics):
  - Per-route latency P50/P90/P99, token/sec, error rate
  - GPU utilization, memory pressure, KV cache hit rate
  - Disk I/O saturation, network egress throttling
  - Alert thresholds: P99 latency > 1.2x target for 5m, error rate > 2% for 10m, GPU temperature > 85C
- Backups:
  - Model artifacts (S3/MinIO) daily incremental, weekly full snapshot.
  - Database (metadata) point-in-time backups every 6 hours; retain 30 days.
  - Restore test: perform quarterly restore drill to a staging environment.

Upgrade procedure (recommended safe path):
1. Review release notes and upgrade matrix in the release manifest; confirm compatibility with on‑prem drivers and KMS.
2. Create a release branch and snapshot current state: export DB schema version and current config `kubectl get configmap/redwood-config -o yaml` or `redwood-config backup`.
3. Canary upgrade: pick 5–10% of worker pool in a non-critical AZ/cluster and apply upgrade with health checks enabled.
4. Monitor for 1–3 hours (or 3x typical codepath latency window) for regressions (latency, errors, memory leaks).
5. If canary is green, roll forward in 20% increments. Use automated rollout with automatic pause on SLO breach.
6. Finalize by upgrading control-plane components and metadata services during low-traffic window.

Automated upgrade commands (example Helm):
# upgrade canary namespace
helm upgrade redwood --namespace redwood-canary ./charts/redwood --set image.tag=2026.02.0
# monitor health
kubectl rollout status deployment/redwood-worker -n redwood-canary --timeout=10m

Rollback procedure (fast recovery):
1. Trigger rollback immediately if canary or staged rollout shows SLO breach or critical errors.
2. If using Kubernetes: `helm rollback <release> <revision>` or `kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name> -n <ns>`.
3. If on-host systemd units: stop new service, restore previous binary/artifact from `/opt/redwood/releases/<previous>` and `systemctl restart redwood-agent`.
4. Restore metadata only when necessary and after coordination — avoid cross-version DB writes. If DB migration ran, use the pre-upgrade DB snapshot and restore to a staging cluster for validation before applying to prod.
5. Post‑rollback: notify stakeholders, open incident for RCA, run regression test suite, schedule a controlled reattempt after root cause fix.

Post‑upgrade validation (smoke tests):
- Run synthetic traffic generator for 10 minutes against representative routes.
- Validate model outputs for a saved prompt set (compare token-level diffs) and check embedding cosine similarity thresholds.
- Verify billing/usage counters and audit logs are incrementing correctly.

Common troubleshooting checklist (quick):
- Service won't start: check journalctl /var/log/redwood/*.log for permission or missing keys.
- Agent not connecting: validate TLS handshake, cert SANs, and firewall rules.
- High latency after upgrade: check kernel driver mismatches, CPU throttling, or new contention introduced by scheduler changes.

Ownership and escalation matrix:
- Deployment lead: Solutions Eng (on call) - pager: @solutions-oncall (Slack)
- SRE escalation: eng-sre@redwood.ai - PagerDuty: SRE team
- Security / Keys: security@redwood.ai

Appendix A - Example K8s resource snippet (worker deployment):
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: redwood-worker
  namespace: redwood
spec:
  replicas: 8
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: redwood-worker
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: redwood-worker
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: worker
        image: registry.redwood.ai/redwood/worker:2026.02.0
        resources:
          limits:
            nvidia.com/gpu: 1
            memory: "120Gi"
          requests:
            cpu: "4"
            memory: "64Gi"

Appendix B - Useful CLI commands:
- Check agent status: `redwood-agent status` or `kubectl get pods -n redwood -o wide`
- Export logs: `kubectl logs deployment/redwood-worker -n redwood --tail 500 > /tmp/redwood-worker.log`
- Trigger manual backup: `redwood-backup --target s3://customer-backups/redwood/$(date +%F)`
